statement: By writing $7+4\sqrt{3}$ in the form $(a+b\sqrt{3})^{2}$ with positive integers $a,b$, show that $\sqrt{7+4\sqrt{3}}=2+\sqrt{3}$. Hence express $\sqrt{7-4\sqrt{3}}$ as a simple surd.
solution: Suppose $(a+b\sqrt{3})^{2}=a^{2}+3b^{2}+2ab\sqrt{3}=7+4\sqrt{3}$. Matching parts gives $a^{2}+3b^{2}=7$ and $2ab=4$, so $ab=2$. With positive integers, $a=2,b=1$ works ($4+3=7$ and $ab=2$). Hence $\sqrt{7+4\sqrt{3}}=2+\sqrt{3}$. For $7-4\sqrt{3}$: $(2-\sqrt{3})^{2}=4-4\sqrt{3}+3=7-4\sqrt{3}$. Since $2>\sqrt{3}$, $\sqrt{7-4\sqrt{3}}=2-\sqrt{3}$.
hints: Match the rational and irrational parts.
